mediaItem.focusTheme_Work: Wrongful conviction, investigative journalism, criminal justice system flaws, personal stories of exonerees.
mediaItem.keyStats:
- America has 2.2 million people in prison.
- Just 1% wrongful conviction rate equals 22,000 people.
- Angel Cordero served 13 years for a crime he did not commit.
- Angel Cordero was released on parole but is not exonerated and is still fighting his conviction.
- 28 eyewitnesses came forward in support of Angel Cordero's innocence after his conviction.
- The actual perpetrator confessed to the crime, but it was deemed not credible by the court.
mediaItem.summaryNotes: This episode of Wrongful Conviction with Jason Flom tells the harrowing story of Angel Cordero, a Bronx man wrongfully convicted of murder and sentenced to 15 years in prison, of which he served 13.  The episode details the night of the crime in 1999, where Cordero and his brother were arrested amidst chaos despite being innocent.  Key issues highlighted include police misconduct, failure to investigate alternative suspects despite eyewitness accounts, prosecutorial misconduct in withholding exculpatory DNA evidence, and ineffective legal counsel.  Despite overwhelming evidence of innocence, including a confession from the actual perpetrator and numerous eyewitnesses, Cordero remains not fully exonerated but was released on parole after years of fighting his conviction. The podcast emphasizes the devastating impact of wrongful convictions on individuals and their families, and the urgent need for systemic reform within the justice system.

featuredIndividual.fullName:
Dario Rodriguez
- Known to police and neighborhood as a repeat offender with arrests dating back to age 14.
- Was apprehended at the scene initially but escaped while police were focused on arresting Angel Cordero.
- Was identified by multiple eyewitnesses as the perpetrator.
- Confessed to the crime in a later hearing, but deemed not credible by the court.
- Had a false alibi claiming he was with his girlfriend the night of the crime, which was later disproven.
featuredIndividual.exonerationYear: Not yet exonerated, released on parole.
contributingFactorsRaw: Eyewitness misidentification (victim identified Cordero 13 months later in court after police suggested they had "gotten the guy").
Police misconduct (beatings, macing, ignoring initial evidence pointing to actual perpetrator, potentially letting the actual perpetrator escape).
Inadequate Legal Defense (Public Defender seemingly unprepared and potentially biased against client's innocence).
Prosecutorial Misconduct (withholding DNA evidence that was exculpatory).
False Alibi of actual perpetrator not properly investigated by police, but later disproven.
featuredIndividual.status: Released on parole (post-release supervision), conviction not overturned, still fighting for exoneration.
organizationsInvolvedRaw: Innocence Project (represented by Barry Scheck and Sima Safi currently).
featuredIndividual.original_trial: Public Defender, described as unprepared and seemingly believing in Cordero's guilt. Name not specified in transcript.
featuredIndividual.appeals:
- Claudia Trapp (Appellate Attorney, name mentioned as “wonderful” and “angel” to Angel).
- Barry Pollack (Appellate Attorney, mentioned taking the case “out of the clear blue sky”).
- Current representation: Barry Scheck and Sima Safi from the Innocence Project.
featuredIndividual.crossReference: Not specified in transcript if in exoneree database, but likely given Innocence Project involvement.
featuredIndividual.narrativeOriginalCrime: A Bronx resident was stabbed and killed by a group of strangers in 1999. Angel Cordero and his brother were arrested at the scene shortly after the stabbing occurred.
keyEvidenceProsecutionRaw: Testimony of three police officers who arrested Cordero and his brother.
Eyewitness identification by the victim, Jason, 13 months after the incident in court.
Prosecution implied victim's blood was on Angel Cordero's clothes at trial.
featuredIndividual.trialDefenderNotes:
- Lawyer seen a couple of times before trial.
- Described as unprepared.
- Did not effectively highlight inconsistencies in eyewitness testimony.
- Failed to present evidence of actual perpetrator or utilize alibi disproof effectively.
featuredIndividual.confession_of_actual_perpetrator_(dario_: Confessed in court during a hearing, detailing the crime. Judge deemed him not credible.
featuredIndividual.eyewitnesses_(28): 28 individuals came forward after conviction stating Cordero was not the perpetrator and identifying Dario Rodriguez.
featuredIndividual.dna_evidence: DNA testing of blood on Cordero’s clothes showed it was his own blood, not the victim’s, contradicting prosecution claims. This evidence was withheld by the prosecution and not presented at trial.
featuredIndividual.alibi_disproof: Dario Rodriguez's alibi was proven false by a nun from a homeless shelter.

keyQuotesRaw: Angel Cordero: "Having to hear those people say that I was guilty of a crime that I did not commit, and then hear my family break down behind me and not be able to do anything about it, I can't describe the crushing weight that was."
Angel Cordero: "I'm not anti-police, I'm just anti-corruption."
Angel Cordero: "A lot of times we look and we see something happen to somebody, and that's the first thing we say, that could never happen to me, but it can."
Jason Flom: "Angel, your case makes no fucking sense whatsoever."
Julio, Pierre, Gregory (arrested with Angel): "We know the guy who did it. We will take you to him. His name is Dario." (Ignored by police).
Michelle Cordero (regarding conjugal visits): "As wonderful as it is, it's so emotionally draining."

Angel Cordero (final thoughts): "Then they made life after that with wild living, that's it. It was all worth it. And I would do it all over again and find new that I was going to get the same, the same two kids waiting for me at the end of the tunnel."
systemicIssuesRaw: Ineffective assistance of counsel (Public Defenders overwhelmed).
Lack of accountability in the justice system.
Difficulty in overturning wrongful convictions even with overwhelming evidence.
policyRecommendationsRaw: Support for organizations like the Innocence Project.
Improved resources and support for Public Defenders.
personalNarrativeRaw: Angel Cordero's 13 years of wrongful imprisonment and ongoing fight for exoneration.
Devastating impact on Cordero’s family, including his mother, brother, daughter and wife Michelle.
Emotional toll of wrongful conviction: loss of time, relationships, opportunities, and mental health.
Michelle Cordero's experience of building a relationship and family with someone wrongfully incarcerated, highlighting the emotional and logistical challenges.
The power of hope, resilience, and love in the face of injustice.
